title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 8.2.1 Reading: Reading Fluency

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Fluent reading is accurate, steady and full of expression, so the listener can follow the meaning. In this sub-strand you will use fluency strategies on a farm text of about 300 words, answer questions that ask you to read between the lines, and bring a short script and a rhyme to life with your voice.

## Strand 8.0: The Farm
Sub-strand 8.2.1: Reading: Reading Fluency
Suggested lessons: 2

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) read a text of about 300 words accurately, at the right speed and with expression for effective communication
b) use fluency strategies to read a text of about 300 words related to the theme to enhance comprehension
c) realise the importance of fluency in reading for comprehension

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is it important to read at a reasonable speed?
2. How can you read a text fast?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: This is enhanced as the learner acquires fluency in reading when they read fast and with appropriate expressions.
• Digital Literacy: It is developed as the learner manipulates the digital device as they read from it or listen to an audio recording.

## Values
• Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner reads from a digital text while observing online safety precautions.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Assertiveness: This is nurtured as the learner develops fluency in reading and expressing themselves without fear.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner applies the knowledge gained in reading fluently to reading which is an aspect in all other learning areas.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 8.0 The Farm, Sub-strand 8.2.1 Reading Fluency

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Reading a farm text with accuracy and expression

LESSON 1: READING A FARM TEXT WITH ACCURACY AND EXPRESSION
==========================================================

## What you will learn
• Read a text of about 300 words accurately and at a steady speed.
• Use phrasing, expression and repeated reading.
• Explain why fluent reading helps understanding.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a text of about 300 words accurately, at the right speed and with expression for effective communication; b) use fluency strategies to read a text of about 300 words related to the theme to enhance comprehension; c) realise the importance of fluency in reading for comprehension

## Introduction
A learner who gallops through a page may say every word and still miss the story. Another learner who stops dead at each word never lets the sentences join up. Fluency is the middle path: accurate, steady and meaningful.

## Notes
### Three parts of fluency
**Accuracy** means you say the words that are really on the page. Guessing harvest when the word is fertilizer changes the facts.

**Rate** means a reasonable speed. Read fast enough for the sentence to sound like speech, and slowly enough for you and your listener to understand. If you race, meaning drops out. If you halt on every word, the story breaks into pieces.

**Expression** means your voice shows the sense. Let your voice fall at a full stop, pause briefly at a comma, and sound interested when something new happens. A question lifts a little at the end.

### Strategies that help
- Look ahead to the end of the phrase, not only at the next letter.
- Read in groups of words: met us at the gate, not met / us / at / the / gate.
- If you stumble, go back to the start of the phrase and try once more.
- Read the same paragraph three times. The third reading is usually smoother. This is called repeated reading.
- When you read from a screen, use a site or file an adult has chosen, and do not click away to unknown links.

Fluency matters because understanding rides on it. A listener cannot picture the tractor, the pests or the meal if the words are scrambled or too fast.

### A Saturday on the Farm
Last Saturday our class visited a farm near the school. The farmer, Mrs Achieng, met us at the gate and asked us to walk slowly so that we would not frighten the hens. She wore boots because the path was wet. First she showed us the vegetable field. Rows of sukuma wiki, tomatoes and onions stood in straight lines. She said the plants need water, sunlight and good soil. A boy asked why some leaves had holes. Mrs Achieng explained that pests such as caterpillars chew leaves. She does not spray carelessly. She picks some pests off by hand and grows indigenous vegetables that do well in our climate.

Next we watched the tractor. It pulled a plough that turned the soil in long brown lines. The driver told us never to run near a moving tractor. We stood behind the fence and only looked. In the shed we saw sacks of seed, a watering can and a wheelbarrow. A girl pointed at a bag of fertilizer. Mrs Achieng said fertilizer feeds the soil, but a farmer must use the right amount. Too much can wash into a river and harm the life in the water.

At noon we sat under a tree and ate mangoes the farm had harvested that morning. They were ripe and sweet. While we ate, Mrs Achieng told us to wash fruit and vegetables before we eat them. Those foods, with grains and beans, help the body grow. On the way home we sang a rhyme about seeds and rain. I wrote three new words in my book: harvest, pests and plough. The visit taught me that food does not appear in the market by itself. Someone plants it, protects it and gathers it with care. We thanked Mrs Achieng before we left.

On a first reading, mark two words you need to look at again. On the second reading, keep those words smooth. On the third, read a paragraph aloud to a partner and ask, Could you picture the farm?

## Key words
• fluency — reading accurately, at a suitable speed and with expression
• accuracy — reading the words that are actually written
• expression — using your voice to show the meaning and the punctuation
• repeated reading — reading the same text several times so it becomes smoother

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner reads fertilizer as factory. What part of fluency has slipped?

Working:
1. The word on the page was not the word that was said.
2. That is a problem of accuracy, even if the speed was fine.

Answer: Accuracy

### Example 2
Where should the voice pause in this sentence? She wore boots because the path was wet.

Working:
1. There is no comma in the middle.
2. The voice falls and pauses at the full stop.

Answer: At the full stop after wet

## Activity: Three readings
You will need: The passage A Saturday on the Farm, A pencil
1. Read the passage silently and underline two words you want to practise.
2. Read one paragraph aloud at a steady speed. A partner follows on the page and notes any word that was changed.
3. Read the same paragraph again with expression, pausing at full stops.
4. Tell your partner one fact you understood better on the second reading.

## Practice
1. Name the three parts of fluent reading.
2. Why did some leaves in the field have holes?
3. What did the driver tell the class about the tractor?
4. Why does reading the same paragraph again help?

## Summary
• Fluent reading is accurate, steady and expressive.
• Phrase words in groups, pause at full stops, and reread.
• Fluency helps both the reader and the listener understand the text.

### Answers to practice
1. Accuracy, a reasonable speed, and expression.
2. Pests such as caterpillars had chewed them.
3. Never to run near a moving tractor.
4. Repeated reading makes the words more accurate and the voice smoother, so the meaning is easier to follow.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Reader's theatre, rhythm and inference

LESSON 2: READER'S THEATRE, RHYTHM AND INFERENCE
================================================

## What you will learn
• Read a part in a reader's theatre with a lively voice.
• Keep the rhythm of a short rhyme.
• Answer direct questions and questions that need an inference.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a text of about 300 words accurately, at the right speed and with expression for effective communication; b) use fluency strategies to read a text of about 300 words related to the theme to enhance comprehension

## Introduction
In a reader's theatre you do not need costumes or a stage. You need the words and a voice that makes a listener see the farm. The script below is for that kind of reading.

## Notes
### Direct questions and inferences
A **direct question** is answered in the words of the text. Who met the class at the gate? Mrs Achieng. The sentence says so.

An **inference** is a conclusion you draw from clues. The text may not state it in one ready sentence. Why did the class stay behind the fence? The driver had warned them never to run near a moving tractor, and the next sentence says they stood behind the fence and only looked. The clue is safety. Why wear boots? The path was wet. What does the writer mean by saying food does not appear in the market by itself? Someone has to plant, protect and harvest it.

When you answer, use a clue from the text and then say what it shows. I know they were careful because they stood behind the fence.

### Reader's theatre
Take turns. Narrator reads the story line. The other parts speak as people.

Narrator: Mrs Achieng met the class at the gate.
Mrs Achieng: Walk slowly. The hens are easily frightened. The path is wet, so step carefully.
Narrator: In the field, a boy pointed at the leaves.
Boy: Why are there holes in these leaves?
Mrs Achieng: Pests have been chewing them. I pick many off by hand. I do not spray carelessly.
Narrator: The tractor pulled the plough.
Driver: Stay behind the fence. Never run near a moving tractor.
Narrator: At noon they ate fruit under a tree.
Mrs Achieng: Wash the fruit and vegetables before you eat them.
Narrator: The class thanked her and left.

Speak so that the warning sounds like a warning and the welcome sounds like a welcome. Look up from the page at the end of a sentence.

### Rhythm in a rhyme
Clap once for each strong beat as you read.

Seed in the soil, rain on the row,
Leaves lift up and the seedlings grow.
Wash what you pick, and share what you know,
Thank the farmer who ploughs the row.

The lines are similar in length, and row, grow, know and row rhyme. Keeping that pattern is another kind of fluent reading. You can sing the rhyme to any simple tune you already know, as long as the words stay clear.

If you listen to a recording, echo one line at a time, then join the lines. Fluent readers sound confident because the words are ready in the mouth. That confidence is built by practice, not by shouting.

## Key words
• reader's theatre — reading a script aloud in parts, using voices instead of costumes or a stage
• inference — a conclusion you draw from clues in the text
• rhythm — a repeated beat or pattern in a poem or song

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Is this a direct question or an inference? What fruit did the class eat at noon?

Working:
1. Look for the exact food in the passage.
2. The text says they ate mangoes.

Answer: A direct question. The answer is mangoes.

### Example 2
Why did the writer thank the people who plant and harvest, not only the market?

Working:
1. The last lines say food does not appear by itself.
2. Someone plants it, protects it and gathers it.

Answer: Because farmers do the work that brings food to the market.

## Activity: Voices on the farm
You will need: The reader's theatre script, The rhyme
1. In groups, give out the parts: Narrator, Mrs Achieng, Boy and Driver.
2. Practise once for accuracy and a second time for expression. No costumes are needed.
3. After the performance, each group answers one direct question and one inference question from the passage.
4. Clap and read the rhyme together, keeping the rhythm steady.

## Practice
1. Who explained the holes in the leaves?
2. Why did the class stand behind the fence instead of running beside the tractor?
3. What is a reader's theatre?
4. Which words rhyme with row in the farm rhyme?

## Summary
• A direct question is answered on the page. An inference uses clues.
• A reader's theatre builds fluency through expressive voices.
• Rhythm and rhyme give the voice a steady pattern to follow.

### Answers to practice
1. Mrs Achieng
2. The driver told them never to run near a moving tractor, so they stayed in a safe place.
3. Reading a script aloud in parts and using your voice to bring it to life, without a set or costumes.
4. grow, know and row
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 8.2.1 READING: READING FLUENCY
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Fluent reading includes accuracy, expression and ________.
   A. shouting
   B. a reasonable speed
   C. skipping lines
   D. closing the book

2. What should you do when you stumble on a phrase?
   A. Close the book
   B. Go back to the start of the phrase and try again
   C. Skip the whole paragraph
   D. Read faster than before

3. Why is repeated reading useful?
   A. It hides mistakes
   B. The text usually becomes more accurate and smoother
   C. It removes the need to understand
   D. It changes the author's words

4. Which crop was NOT named in the vegetable field?
   A. Sukuma wiki
   B. Tomatoes
   C. Onions
   D. Mangoes

5. What can happen if too much fertilizer is used?
   A. It always makes fruit sweeter the same day
   B. It can wash into a river and harm the life in the water
   C. It turns the tractor off
   D. It removes the need to plant

6. Why did Mrs Achieng wear boots?
   A. The path was wet
   B. The hens were noisy
   C. The mangoes were sweet
   D. The shed was locked

7. The class stood behind the fence. What can you infer?
   A. They were hiding from the farmer
   B. They were obeying the driver and staying safe
   C. The tractor was inside the shed
   D. They did not want any fruit

8. Food does not appear in the market by itself. What does the writer mean?

9. What does a reader's theatre need most?
   A. Costumes and a painted set
   B. Voices that bring the script to life
   C. A tractor
   D. A microphone in every hand

10. Why does fluent reading help comprehension?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 8.2.1 READING: READING FLUENCY
========================================

1. B. a reasonable speed
   Rate, or a reasonable speed, is the third part of fluency beside accuracy and expression.

2. B. Go back to the start of the phrase and try again
   Returning to the start of the phrase repairs the mistake without breaking the meaning.

3. B. The text usually becomes more accurate and smoother
   Reading the same text again helps accuracy, pace and expression.

4. D. Mangoes
   Mangoes were the fruit eaten at noon. The field had sukuma wiki, tomatoes and onions.

5. B. It can wash into a river and harm the life in the water
   Mrs Achieng says too much fertilizer can wash into a river and harm the life in the water.

6. A. The path was wet
   The text says she wore boots because the path was wet.

7. B. They were obeying the driver and staying safe
   The driver had just warned them not to run near the moving tractor.

8. Someone has to plant, protect and harvest the food before it can be sold.
   The next sentence says someone plants it, protects it and gathers it with care.

9. B. Voices that bring the script to life
   A reader's theatre uses expressive reading. It does not need a set or costumes.

10. When the words are accurate and the pace is steady, the reader and the listener can follow the meaning.
   Understanding is lost if words are wrong or the voice rushes or stalls.
